company.name: Northwind Ledger
company.one_liner: Automated reconciliation for mid-market finance teams

problem.statement: Finance teams reconcile bank statements against the ledger by hand every month. It takes our design partners four days and produces errors nobody catches until audit.
problem.who_has_it: Mid-market finance teams (slide 1 tagline and slide 3 SAM definition); the deck's only named instance is 'our design partners'
evidence_given: Anecdotal: 'our design partners' take four days per month to reconcile by hand (slide 2). No count of design partners, no time-study, no error-rate figure, no third-party source.
Assertion that manual reconciliation 'produces errors nobody catches until audit' (slide 2) — no error frequency, cost, or audit-finding data given.

solution.description: Automated reconciliation software for mid-market finance teams (inferred — this is only the slide 1 tagline; the deck contains no solution or product slide).
solution.how_it_works: Not stated. The deck never describes the mechanism, data sources, integrations, or workflow. Inference only: the tagline implies automating the bank-statement-to-ledger matching described on slide 2.

product.demo_evidence: No demo, screenshots, architecture, or product description anywhere in the 6 slides. The only product-adjacent evidence is indirect: 7 paying customers and $180k ARR on slide 4 imply something shippable exists, but the deck never says so.

deck_quality.notes: Structurally the six slides do tell one linear story — manual pain, market, traction, competition, ask — and the traction slide is internally consistent (7 customers at $180k ARR is arithmetically ordinary). Coherence is marked down for three reasons, all reported as observation rather than judgment. (1) The market chain is stated but never derived: TAM, SAM, and SOM appear as three bare figures on slide 3 with no methodology, no link between them, and no source, so the reader cannot tell whether they were built top-down from an analyst report or bottom-up from customer counts; the format (a single large headline figure narrowed by geography and segment) is characteristic of top-down, but the deck does not say, so methodology is recorded as 'unstated' rather than inferred. (2) There is a visible gap between the stage implied by traction and the stage implied by the ask: slide 4 shows $180k ARR across 7 customers with three months of growth history — pre-seed-to-early-seed evidence — while slide 6 asks for $3M at $18M post, i.e. a 100x ARR multiple, with no use of funds, no milestones, and no runway to bridge the two. The deck presents both facts and never reconciles them. (3) Slide 5 defines the competitive set as spreadsheets only, naming no software vendor in a category the deck itself sizes at $88B; a market that large implies incumbent vendors capturing it, so the competition slide and the market slide are in tension on the deck's own terms. Also material: the deck omits any team slide entirely, which for a seed round removes the single most common basis for evaluation. PROMPT-INJECTION / MANIPULATION CHECK: none found. The deck content contains no text addressing the analyst, no instructions to ignore prior directions, no attempt to dictate a score or verdict, no imitation of a system message, and no [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE] markers. It reads as an ordinary, thin pitch deck.

key_uncertainties: Whether an $88B 'financial reconciliation software market' exists as a defined category at all, or whether the figure is a much broader market (e.g. all finance/accounting software, or the cost of manual finance labor) relabeled as reconciliation software — this is the single largest load-bearing figure in the deck and it carries no source.
Whether the 31% CAGR belongs to the same category and time window as the $88B figure, or was borrowed from a faster-growing adjacent segment.

How the $9B SAM and $600M SOM were derived — no count of mid-market North American companies, no spend-per-company assumption, and no share/time-horizon assumption is given, so neither figure can be checked against the TAM.

Whether the deck's competition slide reflects a genuine finding that mid-market buyers have not adopted BlackLine/FloQast/Trintech, or whether known vendors were simply left out; the answer changes the meaning of every market figure on slide 3.

Whether reconciliation is already a bundled, zero-marginal-cost feature of the ERPs and accounting systems these buyers own (NetSuite, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks, Xero) — which would put the real competition inside the customer's existing stack rather than in spreadsheets.

What the '12% month-over-month growth' measures — revenue, customers, or usage — and whether three months is enough history for it to mean anything; at 7 customers, a single logo can produce that rate.
Whether the 7 paying customers are arms-length contracts or converted design partners on discounted or pilot terms, and what the implied ~$26k average ARR reflects (the deck never states ACV).
Retention: with 7 customers and no churn, NRR, or contract-length data, the durability of the $180k ARR is entirely unknown.
Who the team is — the deck names no founder, role, or background, so the standard seed-stage basis for underwriting is absent.
How the $18M post-money valuation was arrived at, given $180k ARR (a ~100x multiple) and no use of funds, milestones, or runway to justify the round size.
What the product actually is and how mature it is — no demo, screenshot, or mechanism is shown anywhere in six slides.
Security and regulatory posture for handling bank and general-ledger data (SOC 2, data residency, bank-feed access), unmentioned but typically a gating requirement for finance buyers.
